title: Atrial myxoma removal (Prof. Dr. Tolga Demir)

overlays.text: No left heart vent: it could break up the tumour
Myxoma is friable: stay away from it
Very thin septum: closed with a pledget
Carotids pressed to protect the brain from air

questions.question: What did the echocardiogram before surgery show?
options: A giant tumour attached to the atrial septum, moving in and out of the mitral valve
A vegetation on the aortic valve
A thrombus in the left atrial appendage
questions.explanation: The echo caption says a giant cardiac tumour (myxoma) attached to the atrial septum was moving in and out of the mitral valve in a 60-year-old woman.

questions.question: Which triad characterises the clinical presentation of cardiac myxoma?
options: Obstruction to blood flow, systemic embolism and constitutional symptoms
Chest pain, hypotension and pulsus paradoxus
questions.explanation: Myxomas obstruct flow (often mitral inflow), embolise, and cause fever, weight loss and anaemia through interleukin-6 production.

questions.question: Which approach is used for this operation?
options: Median sternotomy through a midline skin incision
questions.explanation: The midline skin incision (label 'Cilt insizyonu') leads to a median sternotomy, which gives access for bicaval cannulation and the right atrium.

questions.question: Why does the surgeon keep exactly to the midline down to the sternum?
options: It is faster to suture the skin
It gives two equal sternal halves for a secure closure and less bleeding
It avoids the internal jugular vein
It is needed for the drains
questions.explanation: A true midline sternotomy gives equal halves that can be wired together securely and bleeds less.

questions.question: Why are the lungs taken off the ventilator during sternal division?
options: So the lungs fall away from the saw and are not injured
questions.explanation: The surgeon asks to 'take the lungs off' while the saw divides the sternum, then to ventilate again.

questions.question: What is given at 5:09, before any cannulation?
questions.explanation: Full heparinisation is required before cannulas are inserted so the blood does not clot in the bypass circuit.

questions.question: What will the team check three minutes after the heparin?
questions.explanation: The ACT shows whether heparin has taken effect before cannulation.

questions.question: What did the surgeon find when the pericardium was opened?
questions.explanation: 'There was quite a lot of pericardial effusion' - the fluid is suctioned away.

questions.question: Which principle governs this operation before the aorta is cross-clamped?
options: Minimal manipulation of the beating heart, to avoid dislodging tumour fragments
Early opening of the left atrium
Placing a left ventricular vent first
questions.explanation: Until the cross-clamp is on, any fragment would embolise straight into the systemic arteries, so the heart is handled as little as possible.

questions.question: What is a purse-string suture used for in cannulation?
options: It holds the cannula and closes the hole when the cannula is removed
It ties off the vessel permanently
questions.explanation: The cannula goes through the centre of the purse string; a snare tightens it, and tying it later closes the opening.

questions.question: Before cannulating, the surgeon asks to be told when the ACT passes which value?
questions.explanation: Here cannulation starts after the ACT passes 300 seconds. Many teams require a longer ACT, often above 400 to 480 seconds, before full bypass.

questions.question: Where is the purse string labelled at 11:45 placed?
questions.explanation: The label reads 'Vena kava superior kanul dikisi': the purse string for the superior caval cannula.

questions.question: What are the snares threaded onto the purse strings for?
options: To tighten around the cannula, securing it and controlling bleeding
questions.explanation: A snare (tourniquet) tightens the purse string around the cannula and holds it in place.

questions.question: Why does the surgeon ask about the blood pressure before aortic cannulation?
options: A lower pressure reduces the risk of tearing the aorta and bleeding
A high pressure is needed to insert the cannula
questions.explanation: Lowering the systolic pressure is a standard safety step for aortic cannulation.

questions.question: Which vessel receives the arterial cannula in this operation?
questions.explanation: Central cannulation: the arterial cannula goes into the ascending aorta through its purse string.

questions.question: When the arterial line is connected to the cannula, what must be avoided?
questions.explanation: Air in the arterial line could be pumped into the patient, so the line and cannula are filled and joined without air.

questions.question: Which vessel is cannulated in this minute?
questions.explanation: The label reads 'Vena kava superior kanulasyonu'.

questions.question: Where is the antegrade cardioplegia needle placed?
options: In the aortic root, between the aortic valve and the cross-clamp
questions.explanation: Antegrade cardioplegia flows from the aortic root into the coronary arteries; retrograde cardioplegia would use the coronary sinus.

questions.question: How does bypass start in this case?
options: With both caval cannulas in place
With only the superior caval cannula draining, before the inferior caval cannula is placed
After the right atrium is opened
questions.explanation: 'Start. One cannula for now.' The inferior caval cannula is added next.

questions.question: What is the purse string placed low on the right atrium for?
questions.explanation: 'The stitch for the inferior cava': it will hold the inferior caval cannula.

questions.question: Why are two venous cannulas (bicaval cannulation) needed here?
options: So the right atrium can be opened while both venae cavae drain to the machine
questions.explanation: With both cavae cannulated and later snared, the right atrium can be opened in a dry field.

questions.question: Why is no left ventricular vent placed through the right superior pulmonary vein?
options: A vent passing through the left atrium could fragment the friable tumour and cause embolism
The pulmonary veins are too small
questions.explanation: 'We may not place a vent here, because I don't want to break up the mass.' The heart is decompressed through the aortic root instead.

questions.question: What will tightening the snares around both venae cavae achieve?
options: It stops caval blood entering the right atrium, giving total bypass and a dry field
questions.explanation: Snared cavae send all venous return into the cannulas, so the right atrium can be opened.

questions.question: During this minute the heart is still beating. What will stop it?
questions.explanation: The cross-clamp isolates the coronary circulation and cardioplegia arrests the heart.

questions.question: How does high-potassium cardioplegia arrest the heart?
options: It depolarises the myocardial cell membrane, causing diastolic arrest and lowering oxygen demand
It hyperpolarises the membrane and causes systolic arrest
It cools the heart to 4 degrees by itself
questions.explanation: Raised extracellular potassium depolarises the membrane and inactivates sodium channels, so the heart stops in diastole. Topical cold saline adds protection while the patient stays normothermic.

questions.question: What happens when the caval snares are tightened at 25:35?
questions.explanation: All venous blood now goes to the machine: 'now we're on full bypass'.

questions.question: Through which chamber does the surgeon first enter the heart?
options: The left atrium through Sondergaard's groove
questions.explanation: A right atriotomy (label 'Atriyotomi') gives access to the interatrial septum.

questions.question: What is the aortic root vent for during the arrest?
options: To decompress the heart and remove blood and air from the aortic root
To return blood to the patient
questions.explanation: The root vent keeps the heart empty and later helps to remove air.

questions.question: Which landmark will the surgeon use to open the septum?
questions.explanation: The fossa ovalis, the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale, is the thinnest part of the septum, and most left atrial myxomas arise near it.

questions.question: Where does the surgeon see the tumour at 29:25?
options: Behind the fossa ovalis, in the left atrium
questions.explanation: 'This is the fossa ovalis. The mass shows behind it.'

questions.question: Why does the surgeon say 'Stay away from the mass'?
options: A myxoma is soft and friable, and touching it can break off fragments that embolise
The mass is calcified and blunts instruments
It is not the real tumour
questions.explanation: Fragments of myxoma can embolise to the brain or other organs, so the tumour is handled as little as possible.

questions.question: Why is the tissue at the tumour's attachment removed too?
options: To leave no tumour behind and lower the risk of recurrence
questions.explanation: 'We'll take this part of the mass too.' Incomplete removal at the attachment is a cause of recurrence.

questions.question: Where was this myxoma attached?
questions.explanation: The echo report and the operation show attachment to the interatrial septum; its stalk is cut there (label 'Miksoma sapinin kesilmesi').

questions.question: Why is saline injected into the left ventricle after removal?
options: To test the mitral valve and make sure no tumour fragment remains
questions.explanation: 'Valve check. We make sure no piece is left inside' (label 'Mitral kapak kontrolu').

questions.question: Why is the septum closed with a pledget?
options: The septal tissue is very thin, and the pledget stops stitches cutting through and leaving a new ASD
To mark the site for echo
questions.explanation: 'Normally it can be closed without a pledget, but the tissue is very thin, so we don't want to create an ASD.'

questions.question: When would the septum need a patch instead of direct closure?
options: When a larger defect is created, for example by excising a full-thickness cuff of septum
Only when the tricuspid valve leaks
questions.explanation: Here only a limited septal incision was made, so it is closed directly (reinforced with a pledget). A full-thickness excision would leave a defect needing a pericardial or synthetic patch.

questions.question: The septal closure separates which two chambers?
questions.explanation: The interatrial septum lies between the right and left atria.

questions.question: What is the main danger of air left in the left heart when it restarts?
options: Air embolism to the brain or coronary arteries
questions.explanation: Air ejected from the left heart can block cerebral or coronary arteries, so careful de-airing is essential.

questions.question: Why are the lungs inflated by hand before the septum is fully closed?
options: To fill the left heart with blood and push out air
To give oxygen to the pump
questions.explanation: Manual ventilation pushes blood through the lungs into the left atrium, displacing air through the septal opening.

questions.question: Why does the surgeon bury the knot?
options: So no thrombogenic material is left exposed on the inner surface
Because the knot is too long
questions.explanation: Exposed knots or pledget material inside the heart can attract clot.

questions.question: How often does a sporadic myxoma recur after complete excision?
options: Uncommonly, in the range of a few percent
Never, so no follow-up is needed
questions.explanation: Recurrence after complete excision of a sporadic myxoma is uncommon (a few percent); familial cases recur more often. Echocardiographic follow-up is recommended.

questions.question: How is the tricuspid valve tested?
options: Saline is injected into the right ventricle and the leaflets are watched as it fills
questions.explanation: 'Look, the heart is swelling. As it swells, the chordae pull' the leaflets together.

questions.question: What was the result of the tricuspid valve test?
options: Only a trace of leak; no repair needed
questions.explanation: 'Only a trace. No repair needed at all.'

questions.question: Which incision is being closed in this minute?
questions.explanation: The label reads 'Sag atriyotominin kapatilmasi'.

questions.question: Why are the carotid arteries pressed when the cross-clamp comes off?
options: To reduce the chance of air reaching the brain
To stop bleeding from the neck
questions.explanation: Compressing the carotids briefly while the root is vented lowers the risk of cerebral air embolism.

questions.question: Which drug is usually given after decannulation to reverse heparin?
questions.explanation: Protamine neutralises heparin once bypass is over and the cannulas are out. In this minute the heart also restarts on its own (label 'Kalbin spontan calismasi').

questions.question: What is used to close the sternum?
questions.explanation: Stainless steel wires are passed around or through the sternum and twisted tight.

questions.question: Why must the sternum be closed firmly?
options: For stable healing, less pain and fewer wound complications
questions.explanation: A stable sternum heals better; an unstable one risks pain, infection and dehiscence.

questions.question: Which layer is closed after the sternum (label at 48:15)?
questions.explanation: The label reads 'Cilt alti dokularinin kapatilmasi': closure of the subcutaneous tissues.

questions.question: How are complete removal and the diagnosis confirmed after surgery?
questions.explanation: Postoperative echocardiography confirms complete removal and normal valve function; histopathology confirms myxoma (stellate cells in a myxoid stroma).

questions.question: When are screening for Carney complex and examination of relatives advised?
options: In familial or atypical cases, such as young patients, multiple or recurrent tumours, or unusual sites
Only if the tumour is in the right atrium
questions.explanation: Carney complex (often a PRKAR1A mutation) causes multiple, recurrent myxomas in younger patients; first-degree relatives should be examined.

questions.question: Where do the chest drains exit?
options: Near the lower end of the incision
questions.explanation: The drains come out through separate small openings near the lower end of the wound.

questions.question: Which statement summarises this operation?
options: The myxoma was removed through the right atrium and septum on bypass, without a left heart vent, and both valves were checked
The tumour was removed through the aorta without bypass
The tumour was left in place and biopsied
questions.explanation: Bicaval cannulation, cardioplegic arrest, right atriotomy, transseptal excision with the stalk, fragment and valve checks, careful de-airing.

narration.text: This film documents the excision of a left atrial myxoma, recorded from the operating surgeon's perspective.
The surgeon is Professor Tolga Demir. Primary cardiac tumours are rare, and myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumour in adults.
The preoperative echocardiogram, in a sixty year old woman, shows a large mass attached to the interatrial septum that prolapses through the mitral orifice in diastole.

This is the classic picture. About three quarters of myxomas arise in the left atrium, usually from the septum near the fossa ovalis. A prolapsing tumour can obstruct mitral inflow and mimic mitral stenosis.

Clinically, myxomas present with a triad: obstruction to blood flow, systemic embolism, and constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss and anaemia, which are linked to tumour production of interleukin six.
Most myxomas are sporadic. A minority are familial, as in the Carney complex, where tumours tend to be multiple, appear in younger patients, and recur more often.
Because of the risk of embolic stroke and sudden valvular obstruction, surgery is advised soon after the diagnosis.
Gowning and draping complete the sterile field. Transoesophageal echocardiography is commonly used in theatre to confirm the attachment site and to guide de-airing later.
An iodine impregnated incise drape covers the chest.
Skin incision. A median sternotomy gives full access to the heart, the great vessels and both venae cavae.
Electrocautery deepens the incision down to the sternum, exactly in the midline.
A true midline division gives two sternal halves of equal width, which is the basis of a stable closure.
Ventilation is suspended during the sternotomy, so the lungs fall away from the saw and the pleura is spared.
Ventilation resumes. The bone looks thin, so the sternal edges are handled gently to avoid a fracture.
Systemic heparin is given, typically three hundred to four hundred units per kilogram, to prevent clotting in the extracorporeal circuit.
Bone wax provides mechanical haemostasis at the cut marrow of the sternum.
The activated clotting time, the A C T, will be measured about three minutes after the heparin, to confirm adequate anticoagulation.
The sternal retractor is opened gradually, which lowers the risk of rib fracture and brachial plexus injury.
Pericardiotomy. The pericardium is opened in the midline.
As the surgeon anticipated, there is a considerable pericardial effusion, which is aspirated.
Pericardial stay sutures suspend the pericardium and elevate the heart into the operative field.

Note the principle that governs this whole operation: minimal manipulation of the heart before the aorta is clamped. Handling the beating heart could dislodge fragments of this friable tumour into the systemic circulation.
Purse string sutures are now placed for cannulation. They secure each cannula, and later close the opening when it is removed.
The first is placed on the distal ascending aorta, for the arterial cannula that returns oxygenated blood from the machine.
The surgeon asks to be told when the A C T exceeds three hundred seconds. Before full bypass, most teams require values above four hundred to four hundred and eighty seconds.
A second purse string is placed on the superior vena cava. Direct caval cannulation, rather than a single atrial cannula, keeps the right atrium free to be opened.
Snares are threaded over the purse strings to secure the cannulas.
With adequate anticoagulation confirmed, cannulation can proceed.
The inferior caval cannula is prepared, and then the aortic cannula.
The systolic pressure is checked. Cannulating the aorta at a lower pressure reduces the risk of aortic dissection and bleeding.
The aortic cannula is inserted, snared and tied.
Aortic cannulation carries a small risk of iatrogenic dissection, so the tip is directed along the lumen and the line pressure is watched.
The arterial line is connected without air. Even small volumes of air in the arterial circuit can cause cerebral air embolism.
The superior vena cava is cannulated, and the cannula is snared and secured.

Consider why bicaval cannulation matters here. With a single atrial cannula, opening the right atrium would let air into the venous line and flood the field. Two snared caval cannulas isolate the right atrium completely.
A cardioplegia cannula is placed in the ascending aorta, proximal to the future cross clamp, for antegrade delivery into the coronary arteries.
Cardiopulmonary bypass begins with superior caval drainage alone.
Meanwhile, a purse string is placed low on the right atrium for the inferior caval cannula.
Partial bypass at this stage unloads the heart while it continues to beat and eject.
With the inferior caval cannula in place, bicaval venous drainage is established.
Venous return is checked and full flow is reached. The lungs are no longer needed for gas exchange, so ventilation stops.

A key decision: no left ventricular vent through the right superior pulmonary vein. A vent passed through the left atrium could fragment the tumour and cause embolism, so the heart will be decompressed through the aortic root instead.
Tapes are passed around both venae cavae. Tightening them will divert all venous return into the cannulas.
The inferior vena cava is dissected carefully, protecting the surrounding structures.
Until the aorta is clamped, any fragment that breaks off would travel straight into the systemic arteries. That is why the heart is handled so little up to this point.
The aortic cross clamp is applied between the aortic cannula and the cardioplegia site.
Pump flow is reduced briefly while the clamp is applied, to protect the aortic wall. Cardioplegia is then infused into the aortic root.

Diastolic arrest follows. High potassium cardioplegia depolarises the myocardial cell membrane and stops electromechanical activity, lowering oxygen demand. Topical cold saline adds protection, while the patient is kept normothermic.
The caval snares are tightened. This is total cardiopulmonary bypass.
Right atriotomy. The right atrium is opened.
If more exposure were needed, the incision could be extended toward the aorta.
Stay sutures retract the atrial wall.
The aortic root vent decompresses the heart, and the cardioplegia line is clamped.
Inside the right atrium, the septal landmarks are identified. The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale, and the thinnest part of the septum.
Alternatives include a left atriotomy through Sondergaard's groove, or a biatrial approach. The transseptal route gives excellent exposure of a septal attachment.
Here is the fossa ovalis, with the tumour visible behind it in the left atrium.
The septum is incised through the fossa ovalis, giving direct access to the tumour and its attachment.
Stay away from the mass. Myxomas are gelatinous and friable, and the villous, papillary type in particular tends to fragment and embolise.
The site of attachment is exposed with a small retractor.
The attachment is excised with the tumour. Complete removal of the base is the main safeguard against recurrence. Many surgeons excise a full thickness cuff of septum and repair it with a patch.
The stalk is divided at its septal attachment.
The tumour is delivered intact, without fragmentation.
The specimen: a lobulated, gelatinous mass with areas of haemorrhage. Histology typically shows stellate myxoma cells in a myxoid stroma rich in glycosaminoglycans.
The left ventricle is filled with saline to test mitral competence and to flush out any loose fragments. The chambers are inspected for residual tumour.
No residual tumour is found, and septal closure begins.
Because the septal tissue is thin, a felt pledget reinforces the suture line. It prevents the sutures from tearing through and creating an iatrogenic atrial septal defect.
The tricuspid valve will also be assessed before the right atrium is closed.
Direct closure is possible here because only a limited septal incision was made. A larger defect would need a pericardial or synthetic patch.
The root vent is paused while the final septal sutures are placed.
Before the left heart is closed, it must be filled and de-aired. Air left behind is ejected when the heart starts to beat, and can reach the coronary or cerebral arteries.
Rewarming begins. Manual lung inflation drives blood from the pulmonary veins into the left atrium, displacing air through the septal opening before the last knot is tied.
A slight head down position directs residual air away from the cerebral circulation.
The knot is buried, so that no thrombogenic material remains exposed to the circulation.
The septal closure is complete.
Recurrence after complete excision of a sporadic myxoma is uncommon, in the range of a few percent, but echocardiographic follow up is recommended.
The tricuspid valve is tested by injecting saline into the right ventricle.
As the ventricle distends, the papillary muscles and chordae bring the leaflets into coaptation.
Only trace regurgitation is seen, so no repair is required.
The right atriotomy is closed.
The heart is filled, and the inferior caval snare is released.
The cross clamp is removed with the aortic root vent on full suction, while the carotid arteries are briefly compressed to reduce the risk of cerebral air embolism.
Coronary reperfusion washes out the cardioplegia, and the heart resumes a spontaneous rhythm.
The patient is weaned from bypass, the cannulas are removed, and protamine is usually given to reverse the heparin.
Mediastinal drains are placed, and haemostasis is confirmed.
The sternum is approximated with stainless steel wires.
Sternal stability is essential for healing. Poor approximation predisposes to dehiscence and deep sternal wound infection.
The subcutaneous tissue is closed in layers, eliminating dead space.
After surgery, echocardiography confirms complete removal and normal valve function, and histopathology confirms the diagnosis.
The skin is closed with a continuous suture.
In familial or atypical cases, screening for the Carney complex and examination of first degree relatives are advised.
The wound is dressed, with the drains exiting below the incision.

To summarise: a left atrial myxoma was excised through a right atrial, transseptal approach, on bicaval cardiopulmonary bypass with cardioplegic arrest. The keys were minimal manipulation, no left heart vent, complete excision of the attachment, inspection for fragments, and meticulous de-airing.
Thank you for watching.
